reason: The Jewish people (the primary 'regular people' featured in the narrative) are portrayed quite favorably throughout the text. They are depicted as brave, unified, and wise, particularly in their collective response to the existential threat posed by Haman's genocide plot. The narrative emphasizes their courage in defending themselves (וַיַּכּוּ הַיְּהוּדִים בְּכָל־ אֹיְבֵיהֶם - 'the Jews struck all their enemies'), their unity in gathering together (נִקְהֲלוּ הַיְּהוּדִים - 'the Jews gathered'), and their ultimate victory and celebration. Mordecai and Esther, though rising to high positions, remain connected to their people and act nobly on their behalf. The text concludes by establishing Purim as a commemoration of Jewish triumph and resilience, with emphasis on acts of charity to the poor (מַתָּנוֹת לָאֶבְיוֹנִים - 'gifts to the poor'). This positive portrayal extends to their growth in honor and respect throughout the realm.
